root.meaning: one who puts things in order
root.note: ordināre ‘to put in order’ + the agent ending -tor. Spanish sees it as ordenar + -dor, but the computing sense came from French.

history: This word marks Spain's border with Latin America. Most of Latin America says computadora, close to English computer. Spain says ordenador, because it followed France. In 1955, IBM France felt calculateur was too narrow for its new machines and asked Jacques Perret, a professor of philology, for a name. In a letter of 16 April he suggested ordinateur, an old word from Latin ordinātor, ‘one who puts in order’. Spanish then took the French idea and could use its own materials: ordenar, ‘to put in order’, + -dor, the ending of machines like destornillador, ‘screwdriver’. So in a Spanish office you sit at un ordenador, whatever your Mexican colleague calls it.
historyEinfach: In Spain, a computer is an ordenador. In most of Latin America, it is a computadora. Why? In 1955, a French professor gave IBM in France a new word for its machines: ordinateur. It comes from Latin and means ‘a person who puts things in order’. Spain followed French. The Latin American word is close to English computer.

elsewhere.text: French is the reason Spain has this word at all. Thank Jacques Perret, and a letter from 1955.
English gave Latin America computadora. Same machine, but it counts instead of putting in order.
